title: Experimental zero-added-loss multiplexing Bell-pair source for long-haul quantum networks
authors: Yoshiaki Tsujimoto, Daiki Ichii, Rikizo Ikuta, Mikio Fujiwara, Masahiro Takeoka, Go Kato, Kentaro Wakui
abstract: Boosting the communication rate of quantum networks is a central challenge in quantum information science. Recently, an efficient entanglement distribution scheme employing quasi-deterministic Bell-pair sources based on time-frequency multiplexing, referred to as zero-added-loss multiplexing~(ZALM), has been proposed. Its implementation, however, requires high-fidelity entanglement swapping across densely multiplexed time-frequency modes, which has remained an experimental challenge. Here we demonstrate entanglement swapping across 16 parallel frequency modes with a high average fidelity of 93.9$\pm$\SI{1.4}{\%}. Notably, polarization-entangled photon pairs in each frequency mode are spectrally single-mode using only off-the-shelf 50-GHz dense wavelength-division multiplexing~(DWDM) filters, eliminating the need for additional narrowband filtering. Furthermore, in order to fully exploit the temporal degree of freedom, the pump pulse is operated with a repetition frequency of \SI{3.0}{GHz}. By combining the frequency and time multiplexing, the total swapping rate reaches 5.38$\pm$0.17\,\si{pairs\,s^{-1}}, which corresponds to the ZALM Bell-pair rate of \SI{8.2e2}{pairs\,s^{-1}}. Our results establish the key experimental capabilities required for ZALM and demonstrate a scalable route toward practical high-rate quantum repeaters and long-haul quantum networks.
summary: This paper presents an experimental demonstration of a Zero-Added-Loss Multiplexing (ZALM) Bell-pair source designed to boost quantum network communication rates. By combining frequency and time multiplexing across 16 modes, the authors achieved high-fidelity entanglement swapping. The results establish a scalable, high-rate source crucial for developing practical quantum repeaters and long-haul quantum communication links.
main_problem: The central challenge addressed is boosting the communication rate of quantum networks by achieving high-fidelity entanglement swapping across densely multiplexed time-frequency modes.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated entanglement swapping across 16 parallel frequency modes with a high average fidelity of 93.9% and achieved a total swapping rate of 5.38 pairs s-1, enabling a ZALM Bell-pair rate of 8.2e2 pairs s-1.
method: The experiment combines frequency and time multiplexing using a Zero-Added-Loss Multiplexing (ZALM) Bell-pair source, utilizing off-the-shelf DWDM filters and operating the pump pulse at a high repetition frequency.
model_or_system: The physical platform is an experimental ZALM Bell-pair source based on Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) in PPLN/Ws waveguides. The system leverages the spectral and temporal degrees of freedom for high-rate entanglement distribution.
key_observables: Average fidelity (93.9% $\pm$ 1.4%), total swapping rate (5.38 $\pm$ 0.17 pairs s-1), and the corresponding ZALM Bell-pair rate (8.2e2 pairs s-1).
important_parameters: 16 parallel frequency modes, 50-GHz DWDM filters, and a pump pulse repetition frequency of 3.0 GHz.
main_assumptions: The necessity of time-resolved detection ($1/f_{	ext{rep}} \gg \Delta	au_j$) is critical for entanglement swapping, and a trade-off exists between spectral bandwidth, spectral purity, and photon loss in frequency multiplexing.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the ZALM architecture, showing concepts for entanglement distribution, the QTX implementation, temporal photon counts at 3.0 GHz, and the joint spectral amplitude. Other figures detail the trade-offs between bandwidths and the relationship between spectral purity and heralding efficiency.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the ZALM concept for high-rate quantum networking, details the experimental implementation involving 16-mode entanglement swapping, and presents measurements confirming the achieved fidelity and rate, establishing a scalable route for quantum repeaters.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum networks, demonstrating a practical, high-rate source of entangled pairs that overcomes key experimental hurdles in multiplexing and entanglement swapping.
